For nnn a positive integer, let σ11(n)\sigma_{11}(n)σ11​(n) denote the sum of the 11th powers of the positive integer divisors of n.n.n. For example if n=pn=pn=p is prime then σ11(p)=1+p11\sigma_{11}(p)=1+p^{11}σ11​(p)=1+p11, so e.g. σ11(2)=2049.\sigma_{11}(2)=2049.σ11​(2)=2049.

In the 1920s, Ramanujan made the following extraordinary observation. Define Δ(q)=q∏m≥1(1−qm)24=q−24q2+252q3−1472q4+⋯\Delta(q)=q\prod_{m\geq1}(1-q^m)^{24}=q-24q^2+252q^3-1472q^4+\cdotsΔ(q)=q∏m≥1​(1−qm)24=q−24q2+252q3−1472q4+⋯ (a modular form) and let τ(n)\tau(n)τ(n) be the coefficient of qnq^nqn for nnn a positive integer (so for example τ(2)=−24\tau(2)=-24τ(2)=−24). Ramanujan proved the very bizarre theorem that τ(n)\tau(n)τ(n) was congruent to σ11(n)\sigma_{11}(n)σ11​(n) modulo 691691691. Examples: 2049+24=3×6912049+24=3\times 6912049+24=3×691, and 1+311−252=256×691.1+3^{11}-252=256\times 691.1+311−252=256×691. The function τ\tauτ is now known as the Ramanujan τ\tauτ-function.

In the 1960s, Serre observed that Ramanujan's theorem (and many other inscrutible congruences involving τ(n)\tau(n)τ(n) modulo various smaller prime numbers such as 23) could be explained by the existence of a family of 2-dimensional ppp-adic representations of the absolute Galois group of Q\mathbb{Q}Q associated to the Δ\DeltaΔ function. This observation was proved by Deligne shortly afterwards, in a 30 page paper which was light on detail, and was later on expanded by Brian Conrad into a 1000-page pdf (no longer available on Brian's website for some reason).

Way back in the early 1900s it was realised that the definition of modular forms could be generalised to Hilbert modular forms, which are to a general totally real number field FFF what modular forms are to Q\mathbb{Q}Q. Deligne's result made people supremely confident of the following folklore conjecture:

Conjecture A: Given a Hilbert modular eigenform, there should be an associated family of 2-dimensional ppp-adic Galois representations of the absolute Galois group of FFF.

Of course it is possible to make precise exactly what I mean by "an associated family" and I will not do this here.

By the time of the Langlands program in the 1960s, the concept of modular form had been generalised to the concept of an automorphic form, and the general conjecture was this:

Conjecture B: If DDD is a quaternion algebra over a totally real field FFF and π\piπ is a cohomological automorphic representation for the reductive group D×D^\timesD×, there should be an associated family of ppp-adic Galois representations ρπ\rho_{\pi}ρπ​ associated to FFF.

Conjecture A is the special case of conjecture B for DDD being the ring of 2×22\times 22×2 matrices over FFF. In fact the general conjecture is that given a large class of automorphic representations π\piπ associated to a general connected reductive group over a general global field, there should exist Galois representations ρπ\rho_{\pi}ρπ​ -- this is the Langlands reciprocity conjecture, proved by the Lafforgues in the function field case and still wide open in the number field case).

A theorem of Jacquet and Langlands from the 1970s showed how to move automorphic representations between different quaternion algebras -- in particular showing that if π\piπ was an automorphic form for D×/FD^\times/FD×/F there was an associated Hilbert modular form, thus essentially reducing Conjecture B to Conjecture A and rendering them equivalent (modulo various edge cases which are not relevant to FLT). But it took a detailed analysis of the cohomology of the associated Shimura varieties and a profound understanding of congruences and pseudorepresentations before humanity (in this case, Richard Taylor) proved the conjectures above. The conjectures were proved in 1989 in a paper which got Taylor tenure in Cambridge UK, and it is not a coincidence that the FLT project is "prove FLT modulo 1980s".

In 2023 when I wrote the FLT proposal, formalising stuff like this was science fiction. In 2026...well...in my mind (but certainly not in everybody else's), it is still science fiction. To those who say "AI can do everything" an easy response is "OK then, do FLT". The answer I get to that is "but FLT is too hard". This is true, and my point is that the conjectures above are also too hard. So then the AI people say "Let us prove that these conjectures will not be too hard next year, please formalize the statements for us".

And this brings me to the problem I face. To formalize Conjecture B, I will need to formalise the definition of a cohomological automorphic representation for the units of a quaternion algebra over a totally real field. It would not surprise me if I could ask Fable or Sol to do this, and a few days later I would have maybe 20000 lines of code containing a mathematically accurate definition. Once one had this, one could state both conjectures A and B, and also the theorem of Jacquet and Langlands showing that they are equivalent. As a bonus, we would also be able to formalise the statement of Langlands' cyclic base change theorem, which is the other major assumption which is blocking a complete proof of FLT.

And now what?

As AI improves I think it's becoming clearer to me what the major obstructions to a full proof of FLT will be in the future, and this post is highlighting what I believe will be all of the most serious ones. There is of course also class field theory (which will be easy using AI) and Mazur's theorem (which will be far less easy, but will be much easier than all this stuff above).

But how does one move forwards here? My original plan, which I have executed already, is to only define the spaces of automorphic forms which I will need for the post-1980s part of the proof, and these are already in FLT. However I think one is forced to make the general definition if one wants to actually get somewhere, and I am not at all clear about how to write a challenge file which is relying on 20000 lines of code which clearly are not going to be in mathlib any time soon.

I have a couple comments about the formalization of Mazur's paper proving the torsion theorem. A little over 20 years ago, I was part of a group of grad students who spent about 16 months reading through it, and while I wouldn't be able to reconstruct the argument if I were asked, I can share some impressions.

First, perhaps the most overwhelming aspect of the paper was the diversity of techniques that were used. In the beginning, it seemed to be a lot of finite flat group schemes, following Raynaud's (p,...,p) paper, then some modular curves and forms following Deligne-Rapoport and Katz, but then Mazur just started pulling things from all over the place, sometimes right in the middle of a proof, like "computation by Lenstra and Van Emde Boas", or Dieudonne modules (citing Oka's unreadable 1964 dissertation), or the Orthogonality Theorem (SGA7). Because of this, I think a formalization following Mazur's path would require a formalization of a surprisingly big chunk of literature, some of which may be hard to decipher. On the other hand, once the theoretical machine is established, some other interesting results (detailed in the last part of Mazur's paper) come mostly for free.

At this point, I would like to draw your attention to my use of the phrase "following Mazur's path", because I ran into Brian Conrad a few times around the time we were doing our reading, and he had a somewhat mixed opinion about the value of spending a lot of time reading Mazur's argument in detail. In particular, he said (if my recollection is correct) that the argument was unnecessarily delicate, and that a treatment with more modern methods could make it much more clear. Unfortunately, I don't have any details about which methods he had in mind, and as far as I can tell, such a treatment has not appeared.

Now, Kevin has suggested a few times in this forum that Mazur's torsion theorem would be a good target for wholesale AI-formalization, and now I see one such attempt is in progress. On the positive side, it may be an interesting test to see if an AI can produce workable API for concepts that we haven't formally defined yet, such as the Neron model of J_0(N) in bad characteristic (I am not particularly optimistic). Also, if an AI could come up with a more modern proof, I could save myself the trouble of writing an email to Brian Conrad.  This is highly nontrivial - I haven't written one despite being curious about a more modern proof for 20+ years. On the negative side, I would just like to say that my own experience struggling with Mazur's paper has given me some kind of emotional attachment, and I am not entirely happy with the way it seems to be tossed out as chum for the Trillion Dollar Zombie.

I have been using Mazur's theorem as protection against the Trillian Dollar Zombie for a while now, indeed I started using it when the AI people were saying "let us just do FLT for you" back when it was clear that the then-current systems were useless. My canonical response at that time was "well let me know when you've done Mazur's theorem because then maybe we're 5% of the way to FLT and you can't actually even do that, can you", which has held up for a while. But now, because I said it, it's become a target (they still can't do it yet, but no doubt they will). I agree with Andrew that all that will happen is that eventually someone will spend a stupid amount of money doing it, it will teach no mathematician anything, but it will teach the formalization community how much time and money goes into formalizing something which is 5% of FLT on (whatever date it falls).

PS maybe 5% is optimistic. 2%? But Theorems A and B upstream are more like 40% (of the proof I'm formalizing -- note that Wiles didn't need them but he needed e.g. Ribet and Langlands--Tunnell, which I don't), with cyclic base change perhaps another 30%.

I think Andrew Snowden's course note is a quite nice exposition of Mazur's torsion theorem. I think he took some shortcuts here and there so I'm not sure if he gets the full strength of Mazur's paper but it is enough to get the torsion theorem. And of course he also cited a bunch of results but almost all of them are one (or perhaps two) book away from mathlib.

As for whether AI can produce workable API for concepts that we haven't formally defined yet: I'd say not yet (at least for now), but a competent human could set up some formal specifications (as statements the new definition should satisfy) and LLMs could work from this point towards both directions: proving more API on top of the and also trying from the ground up to prove the formal spec.

Vasily Ilin said:

I can see your argument being applied to any AI formalization of a known theorem. Do you believe that any AI formalization is similarly useless? To me "we fully formalized FLT" is much more satisfactory than "we formalized FLT modulo the following unformalized but believed to be true results".

It may be a surprisingly unpopular opinion but I am indeed worried that there are holes in published mathematics. That's a big part of why we do formalization.

Traditionally (pre-AI), most of the value in a large formalization project (or, for that matter, a small formalization project) was in the understanding gained (both of the underlying mathematics and of how best to represent mathematics in Lean) and the additions to mathlib resulting. Note also that:

  • Much of this value was gained long before the project was finished (even if it never got very far towards the main result, there were probably still useful additions to mathlib), and continued being gained long after it proved the main result (as material was gradually moved into mathlib afterwards, since mathlib review for large projects has long been slow).
  • Of course the results in those projects tended to be well-established (so little doubt about their truth or validity of the existing proofs - with a few exceptions such as Con(NF)) and to have proofs much shorter than that of FLT, so "making sure there are no holes" wasn't significant value (unlike for a newly proved result, where "has a full Lean proof" may be becoming a basic minimum for it to be worth humans looking at a reported AI proof at all).
  • Value gained by being added to mathlib aligned well with traditional open source software norms. Not "throw my fork out there on GitHub, don't care if anyone uses it" but "I've benefited from all the work other people have put into this open source project (mathlib), now I have a moral responsibility to try to contribute back my work just like all those previous contributors did so in future it works better for everyone, covering my use cases as well as everyone else's".

Now the community has bifurcated. The traditional collaborative community building mathematical understanding and mathlib as a formal Bourbaki is still there, but there's also all the "only care about being sorry-free, don't try to contribute back to mathlib even for lemmas filling small API gaps in existing areas, don't feel any moral responsibility to give back to the projects whose work you're building on" AI-generated code, tending into "AI companies only concerned with showing off how clever their AIs are, dumping multi-MB proofs in a single file".

There are things in between the two extremes as well, such as Tau Ceti, though from the traditional perspective, the main measure of value for Tau Ceti is whether people figure out ways to use it as a staging area where AI-generated code is improved to mathlib standards and upstreamed to mathlib in the process, building understanding in the process.

The problem of large open source users acting as freeloaders, rather than holding up to their side of the social contract and giving back, is of course not something that started with AI.

Scott Carnahan said:

In particular, he said (if my recollection is correct) that the argument was unnecessarily delicate, and that a treatment with more modern methods could make it much more clear.

One place where better technology makes for a slicker argument is in Mazur's proof that the Jacobian of X_0(p) admits a nontrivial rank zero quotient if p>13 (and thus X_0(p) only has finitely many rational points). Mazur's original proof used the "Eisenstein quotient" to do this (and Snowden's proof also uses the Eisenstein quotient) but Merel popularised the use of the "winding quotient", which is bigger -- it is the largest quotient of J_0(p) whose L-function doesn't vanish at 1 -- because by the 1990s we could prove that if the L-function of a modular abelian variety doesn't vanish at 1 then the variety had rank zero, a result not available to Mazur. Of course here one could simply look at Merel's paper (which proves much more -- it proves a version of Mazur's theorem for all number fields).

Unfortunately, I don't have any details about which methods he had in mind, and as far as I can tell, such a treatment has not appeared.

As well as Merel there is work of Calegari and Emerton reinterpreting some of the arguments with the hindsight of a post-R=T world. However R=T is another kettle of fish, and one would have to check that Yang's formalization covered the theorem they use to go down this route (Yang proved the R=T theorem which I need, modulo some assumptions; other R=T theorems need other assumptions, some of which might be very hard (e.g. Ribet).

Mazur's 78 Inventiones paper on isogenies also provided a shorter proof of the torsion theorem via formal immersions (specifically Prop 3.1, that the map from X0(p)X_0(p)X0​(p) to the Eisenstein (nowadays winding) quotient) is a formal immersion. It's used to show that elliptic curves supporting an isogeny have everywhere (away from 2) potentially good reduction (Corollary 4.4), and from there it's a short paragraph argument (see page 146) to get that if ppp is a prime for which there is an elliptic curve with a rational ppp-isogeny, then p≤17p \leq 17p≤17, which from previous results was enough to deduce the torsion theorem. Perhaps (i'm not sure) this result on irreducibility of the mod-ppp Galois representation is all that FLT really needs.

Another decent reference is the appendix of Bilu--Parent's Annals paper where they prove the split Cartan case of Serre uniformity, this incorporates the Merel way of thinking about formal immersions as linear independence of Hecke operators (actually goes back to an 1992 IMRN paper of Kamienny)

Joseph Myers said:

The problem of large open source users acting as freeloaders, rather than holding up to their side of the social contract and giving back, is of course not something that started with AI.

Many people (both before and using AI) have attempted to contribute to Mathlib, but have had their contributions refused.

Contributing to large, established open source projects in general, and to mathlib in particular, is indeed a skill that needs to be acquired. It does require sublimating the immediate motivation of oneself or one's company (providing formalized evidence for the validity of a particular proof, for example) into longer-term building of infrastructure of broader use (giving back to the tools and libraries on which one relied to be able to achieve one's immediate goal in the first place), working together with the community to find the best way to formalize each element used in the proof in suitable generality and possibly going down many rabbit holes of generalization in the process. And it does take a long time, but so does the process of getting an informal proof refereed and revised and formally published, for example; the work on an informal proof is also very far from done when the first version of the preprint is released.

AI companies have many very smart people, near-infinite financial resources, and near-infinite compute power on the latest internal AIs smarter than those available to the public. I'm sure they're able to learn how to work with the mathlib community to contribute to mathlib everything in their formalizations that's of more general use outside the context of the solution to a single problem.

Furthermore, the rate at which changes get reviewed and integrated into mathlib provides a natural limit on the amount of work this expects of AI companies, since they can only reasonably be expected to contribute pieces to mathlib as fast as the dependencies of those pieces get reviewed and integrated. (Until those people gain enough expertise to become reviewers themselves and so reviewers from different AI companies helping to review each others' work also help increase the speed at which changes get reviewed and integrated.)
